module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 930

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/930](https://www.erdosproblems.com/930)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Finset

namespace Erdos930

/--
$n$ is a perfect power if there exist natural numbers $m$ and $l$
such that $1 < l$ and $m^l = n$.
-/
def IsPower (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ m l, 1 < l ∧ m^l = n

/--
Is it true that, for every $r$, there is a $k$ such that
if $I_1,\ldots,I_r$ are disjoint intervals of consecutive integers,
all of length at least $k$, then
$$
  \prod_{1\leq i\leq r}\prod_{m\in I_i}m
$$
is not a perfect power?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_930 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ r > 0, ∃ k, ∀ I₁ I₂ : Fin r → ℕ,
      (∀ i : Fin r, 0 < I₁ i ∧ I₁ i + k ≤ I₂ i + 1) →
        (∀ i j : Fin r, i < j → I₂ i < I₁ j) →
          ¬ IsPower (∏ i : Fin r, ∏ m ∈ Icc (I₁ i) (I₂ i), m) := by
  sorry

/--
Returns the least prime satisfying $k \le p$
-/
def nextPrime (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.find (Nat.exists_infinite_primes k)

/--
Let $k$, $l$, $n$ be integers such that $k \ge 3$, $l \ge 2$ and $n + k \ge p^{(k)}$,
where $p^{(k)}$ is the least prime satisfying $p^{(k)} \ge k$.
Then there is a prime $p \ge k$ for which $l$ does not divide
the multiplicity of the prime factor $p$ in $(n + 1) \ldots (n + k)$.

Theorem 2 from [ErSe75].

[ErSe75] Erdős, P. and Selfridge, J. L., The product of consecutive integers is never a power. Illinois J. Math. (1975), 292-301.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_930.variants.consecutive_strong :
    ∀ k l n, 3 ≤ k → 2 ≤ l → nextPrime k ≤ n + k →
      ∃ p, k ≤ p ∧ p.Prime ∧
        ¬ (l ∣ Nat.factorization (∏ m ∈ Icc (n + 1) (n + k), m) p) := by
  sorry

/--
Erdos and Selfridge [ErSe75] proved that the product of
consecutive integers is never a power (establishing the case $r=1$).

Theorem 1 from [ErSe75].

It is implied from `erdos_930.variants.consecutive_strong`.

[ErSe75] Erdős, P. and Selfridge, J. L., The product of consecutive integers is never a power. Illinois J. Math. (1975), 292-301.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_930.variants.consecutive_integers :
    ∀ n k, 0 ≤ n → 2 ≤ k →
      ¬ IsPower (∏ m ∈ Icc (n + 1) (n + k), m) := by
  sorry

end Erdos930

reformulations.difference: The source quantifies over arbitrary disjoint intervals. Lean restricts their indexing to left-to-right order, encodes the minimum length by I₁ i + k ≤ I₂ i + 1, and does not separately require the existential threshold k to be positive.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k > 0, a + k ≤ b + 1 is equivalent to k ≤ (Finset.Icc a b).card. Any family of disjoint nonempty intervals can be sorted by its lower endpoints; disjointness then gives bᵢ < aⱼ whenever i < j, and reindexing preserves the product. Conversely, such ordered intervals are pairwise disjoint. Any witness threshold can be increased to k + 1, so explicitly requiring a positive threshold changes nothing. The full equivalence between these ordered and unordered threshold formulations was proved as Review930.threshold_iff in /workspace/review/reformulation.lean, without using the file's sorry-backed theorems.

sources_consulted: https://erdosproblems.com/latex/930 (read through its r.jina.ai text view)

Erdős and Selfridge, The product of consecutive integers is never a power, Illinois J. Math. 19 (1975), 292–301; especially the introduction and Theorems 1–2 on p. 292. https://renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1975-46.pdf

Erdős, Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive integers and related questions, Congressus Numerantium XVI (1976), 25–44; equation (9) and surrounding discussion on p. 28. https://renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1976-39.pdf
https://erdosproblems.com/latex/363 (the square-product variant linked by problem 930; read through its r.jina.ai text view)
https://renyi.hu/~p_erdos/Erdos.html (bibliographic index used to locate the primary papers)
review.notes: All five declarations were checked. Both solved variants match Theorems 1 and 2 of the 1975 paper, including its standing convention n ≥ 0. The current problem page confirms that the main question remains open. IsPower includes 0 and 1, but this does not change the claims: the threshold may be increased to at least 2, after which the relevant positive interval products exceed 1. Lean experiments verified nextPrime's least-prime specification, interval cardinalities and positivity, factorization boundary behavior, and small instances of the stronger theorem. Both scratch files compile successfully; the equivalence proofs contain no sorry dependencies.
